column4: This verse explicitly says that those striving with wealth and lives are not like those who stay behind, then says “وَكُلًّا وَعَدَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلْحُسْنَىٰ.” It joins giving, al-husnā, and the promise in one formulation.
This neighbor expands the promised good in 4:95 into degrees, forgiveness, and mercy. It adds the form of reward attached to the same striving with wealth and lives.
The parable is explicitly about spending in God’s way: one seed yields many times its amount. It makes the section’s present gift for a future return concrete as multiplied reward.
Those who spend and do not follow it with reminders or injury have their reward with their Lord. This gives a specific form to giving without seeking repayment from the recipient.

The spenders here seek God’s approval (“ٱبْتِغَآءَ مَرْضَاتِ ٱللَّهِ”) and firm their own souls; the garden parable ties that motive to a secure result, like the section’s gift seeking the Lord’s face.

Believers are told to spend from God’s provision before a Day with no trade or friendship. It makes the section’s “give now for the end” concrete and removes human exchange as a way to secure that end.
This ayah says people will return to God and each soul will be paid in full for what it earned. It places the section’s root ج ز ي and second-life recompense at the return to God.
God does not wrong even an atom’s weight and multiplies good deeds, giving a great reward. It illustrates the section’s account of compensation as a real return that can exceed the deed.

God has bought the believers’ lives and wealth in exchange for the Garden (“بِأَنَّ لَهُمُ ٱلْجَنَّةَ”) and calls it a true promise. This is a direct promise-and-gift formulation of the section’s image.
The one who desires the Hereafter, strives for it as it deserves, and believes has effort appreciated (“مَّشْكُورًۭا”). It connects present action and belief to an accepted future end.

People are called to spend, some withhold, and whoever withholds does so against himself; God is self-sufficient while people are needy. This directly reverses the section’s giver and the miser who thinks himself independent.
After the feeding and refusal of human payment in 76:8–9, the givers explain that they fear a grim Day from their Lord. This names the future judgment that gives their present act its direction.
God protects this group from that Day and gives them radiance and joy. It completes the reward of the selfless givers in 76:8–10 and makes the section’s final satisfaction visible.
The same group is rewarded for patience with a Garden and silk (“وَجَزَىٰهُم بِمَا صَبَرُوا۟ جَنَّةًۭ”). This supplies the Paradise meant by the section’s al-husnā.

The passage closes, “إِنَّ هَـٰذَا كَانَ لَكُمْ جَزَآءًۭ وَكَانَ سَعْيُكُم مَّشْكُورًا”: the gift-givers’ effort is appreciated and rewarded, joining their act to the section’s promised satisfaction.
This asks whether people should be guided to a trade that saves them from painful punishment. The trade image frames the next ayah’s commitment and reward as a return on present action.
The trade in 61:10 is belief and striving with wealth and lives. That specific costly commitment parallels the section’s giving for the promised end; 61:12 supplies the reward.
The promised return for the trade in 61:10–11 is forgiveness and Gardens. It makes the afterlife reward in that transaction explicit.

This directs giving to relatives, the poor, and the traveler, and names seeking God’s face as the motive. It is another specific instance of the section’s giving for God rather than a person’s repayment.

The disbelievers are called the worst of creation and assigned to Hell; 98:7 names the believers the best of creation and 98:8 gives their mutual satisfaction. This supplies the adverse side of that neighboring reward scene.
Believers who do good are called “خَيْرُ ٱلْبَرِيَّةِ,” the best of creation. The next ayah gives their Garden and mutual pleasure, linking the section’s al-husnā to those who believe and act.
For those who believe and do good, this ayah promises “طُوبَىٰ لَهُمْ وَحُسْنُ مَـَٔابٍۢ,” blessedness and a good return. It directly states the good final outcome behind al-husnā.

The verse describes the recompense for evil as its like, then says that whoever forgives and reconciles has reward with God. It concretely shows the section’s root ج ز ي reaching both punitive and rewarding outcomes.

Every soul is paid its reward in full on Resurrection Day; success is entering the Garden and failure is the deluded life of this world. This directly joins the section’s last-life recompense to opposed outcomes.

The saved speaker says, “إِنِّى مُلَـٰقٍ حِسَابِيَهْ,” that he expected to meet his account. It gives a concrete instance of expectation proven in the later reckoning, as in the section’s account of ص د ق.
The saved person is in “عِيشَةٍۢ رَّاضِيَةٍۢ,” a pleasing life. It gives a positive outcome of satisfaction alongside the section’s promised رضى; 69:22 identifies the Garden.
The saved person’s outcome is a high Garden (“جَنَّةٍ عَالِيَةٍۢ”), the Paradise gloss the section gives for al-husnā; it completes the pleasing life of 69:21.
The saved are told to eat and drink in satisfaction for what they sent ahead in past days (“بِمَآ أَسْلَفْتُمْ”). It directly links present action to later satisfaction.
The condemned person says, “مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّى مَالِيَهْ,” that his wealth did not avail him. This is the section’s withheld wealth reaching its opposite outcome; 69:29 says his authority is gone.
The condemned person says his authority has perished (“هَلَكَ عَنِّى سُلْطَٰنِيَهْ”), completing 69:28’s failure of wealth to help him and reversing the giver’s assured end.
This describes the one who preferred the worldly life (“وَءَاثَرَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا”), a specific counterpart to choosing present possession over the section’s better last end.
The person who fears standing before his Lord and restrains the soul from desire (“خَافَ مَقَامَ رَبِّهِۦ”) fits the section’s God-fearing giver; 79:41 supplies the Garden that is his refuge.
This neighbor names the God-fearing person’s refuge as the Garden, completing the contrast with 79:38 and the section’s al-husnā as Paradise.

The one who seeks the harvest of the Hereafter has it increased, while the one who seeks the world’s harvest receives no share in the Hereafter. The present labor/future return and opposed aims make a specific parallel to the section.
The verse tells each soul to look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow (“مَّا قَدَّمَتْ لِغَدٍۢ”) while fearing God. It states the section’s present act measured against the coming end.
Believers are told to spend from what God provided before a Day without trade or friendship. Like 2:254, it ties present giving to a future in which people cannot settle accounts with one another.
The God-fearing are led in groups to the Garden and welcomed through its opened gates. This begins the final-home scene that 39:74 describes as God’s fulfilled promise.

The Garden’s people say God fulfilled His promise to them and gave them the land to inherit; it is called an excellent reward for workers. This directly stages the promise’s fulfillment and satisfied recipient.
God removes the worst of the righteous people’s deeds and rewards them according to “بِأَحْسَنِ مَا كَانُوا۟ يَعْمَلُونَ.” This repeats the section’s better-than-deed measure for recompense.
Believers are told to spend from what God has made them successors over, and those who believe and spend receive a great reward. It links entrusted wealth to the section’s promised end.

The verse distinguishes those who spent before victory from those who spent later, then says good is promised to all. It makes the timing of the section’s “give today” detail consequential while preserving the shared promise.

Those who migrate for God and are killed or die are promised good provision (“رِزْقًا حَسَنًۭا”). Their loss in God’s cause followed by divine provision parallels giving up what one has for the good end.
God promises to admit them to an entry “يَرْضَوْنَهُۥ,” one that pleases them. The return to رضى links this promised entry to the section’s final satisfaction.
Believers who do good are promised Gardens, and the ayah calls this God’s true promise (“وَعْدَ ٱللَّهِ حَقًّۭا”). It names the assurance the section says the giver confirms by action.

This says outcomes are not by wish: whoever does evil is recompensed for it, while the believing doer of good enters the Garden. It directly ties the section’s opposed belief and action to opposite ends.
The righteous spend in ease and hardship (“يُنفِقُونَ فِى ٱلسَّرَّآءِ وَٱلضَّرَّآءِ”). This supplies a concrete giving practice among those promised the Garden; 3:136 names their reward.
The reward of the people described in 3:134 is forgiveness and Gardens. It completes the connection between their spending and the section’s promised final good.
